lines.text: In nineteen thirty-two, Australia declared war
on twenty thousand emus.
The emus won.
See, soldier-settlers were farming wheat in Western Australia,
when twenty thousand emus marched in after breeding season,
trampling the crops and smashing straight through fences.
The farmers begged the army for help,

lines.caps: so the army | sent | Major Meredith, | two | machine guns,
lines.text: so the army sent Major Meredith, two machine guns,
and ten thousand rounds of ammunition.
Simple plan. The emus had other plans.
They scattered into tiny groups and zigzagged
at fifty kilometres an hour.
You can't surround an enemy that just runs around you.

lines.caps: Then | 1,000 emus | strolled | past the guns.
lines.text: Then a thousand emus strolled past the guns.
The soldiers fired, dropped a dozen emus...
and then the gun jammed.
So they bolted a gun onto a truck and gave chase.
The truck ended up in a tree.
By December, the army gave up:
ten thousand rounds, for maybe a thousand birds.
Meredith said these birds could out-tank tanks.

lines.caps: And the emu | today? | It's on | Australia's | coat of arms.
lines.text: And the emu today? It's on Australia's coat of arms.
Winner's podium, mate.

sources: Australian War Memorial encyclopedia, 'Emu War' (awm.gov.au/articles/encyclopedia/emu-war): in November 1932 Major G.P.W. Meredith of the Royal Australian Artillery's 7th Heavy Battery led a small unit with Lewis machine guns against emus damaging farms around Campion, Western Australia; the operation was withdrawn in December 1932

Johnson, 'Feathered Foes: Soldier Settlers and Western Australia's Emu War of 1932', Journal of Australian Studies (2006), and National Archives of Australia defence correspondence: about 20,000 emus migrated into the wheat belt after breeding season, trampling crops and breaking fences; Defence Minister George Pearce approved military assistance with two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds

Cross-checked accounts (AWM records summaries): on 4 November 1932 about 1,000 emus were engaged, roughly a dozen were shot before a gun jammed; emus scatter into small groups and can run at up to 50 km/h; a machine gun was mounted on a truck for pursuit and the truck crashed; total emu kills for the operation are usually put at roughly 1,000 (often 986) for about 10,000 rounds fired; Meredith compared the emus' resilience to tanks
The emu appears on the Commonwealth Coat of Arms of Australia alongside the kangaroo
title: The Army That Lost to Emus
